articles.text: Our spirits are alternately raised and dampened by the conflicting reports of the war talk between England and Russia. There is no use denying the patent fact that this war will be of vast benefit to the United States. With hearty good-will do we see war-like measures inaugurated.
articles.summary: Editorial welcoming the prospect of war between England and Russia as a benefit to the United States.

articles.text: The latest news of the condition of Gen'l. Grant is very favorable as far as his present condition is concerned but as cheerless as ever in reference to the future. The latest examinations seem to have conclusively proved that the disease is a cancer and this must at no distant time end his life. Should he improve he will be taken to Saratoga and thence to the Catskills.
articles.summary: Editorial note that Gen. Grant's cancer is expected to end his life before long.

articles.text: Medora will see better times this summer even than it has had up to the present. The slaughter-house will employ about a hundred men and several times that number will have steady work outside. It is altogether probable that this year and if not, then next, there will be built here a tannery, glue works and other factories to use up the parts of cattle not fit for beef. Not a particle of the animal will be wasted that can possibly be utilized. In fact the business will be conducted on the economical principles of the Chicago slaughter-houses. Several other industries are bound to arise here and altogether Medora can look forward not only to a continuation but to an increase in her prosperity.
articles.summary: Editorial predicting that the slaughter-house will employ about a hundred men and that a tannery, glue works and other factories will follow.

articles.headline: Explanations Wanted.
articles.text:
We wish again to call attention to a matter that has heretofore gone without explanation. It is in reference to the man arrested by Wm. Jones for setting fire to the prairie.

The facts in the case are briefly these. Last fall a man was found near Scoria who had built a fire and allowed it to spread. When spoken to on the subject, he returned an insulting answer and refused to put out the fire. Jones was then asked to arrest the man and put out the fire which he did. The man was kept here a few days and Jones then took him to Mandan for trial. Just as they were getting on the train, the man unsuccessfully tried to bribe Jones to liberate him, showing that he had money. Arrived in Mandan, the man was tried, his guilt clearly proven and he was bound over to the circuit court and as he could not furnish the $200 bail he was put in jail. His crime, by the way, was punishable with a fine of $200 or six months in jail, so it will be seen that the bail was certainly small enough.

In the jail, the prisoner was put at all sorts of jobs and as near as we can make out, became tired of his surroundings and walked away one day.

There has been much comment on this case and no one as yet has been able to learn any particulars as to the man's release. Of course, all put the worst construction on the case and state with a good show of truth that the man put up all the money he had to parties in the ring and he was turned loose. We have no means of knowing whether this is so or not and we write this article with the intention of finding some sort of an explanation.

Somehow and by some legal officer a crime was committed in allowing the criminal to escape. At some time also, Billings county will be called on to pay a large bill in this farce. We propose to know before that bill is paid whether it is a just one or not. If not, it will as surely not be paid as that the COW BOY is published in Medora.

The history of county government in Dakota is blackened all over with crimes committed by legalized robbers in the garb of county officers and as far as Billings county is concerned we propose it shall stop before it has fairly begun.

This remark may not apply to the case in hand, but it looks mightily like it. Under no circumstances except the death or insanity of the criminal could he have been liberated legally. He must have stood trial at the circuit court, which has not yet set.

To stop all further comment on this question we would like to have an answer from the officers interested and will cheerfully make room for their communications.

A marked copy of the COW BOY will be sent to the justice who tried the case, to the prosecuting attorney and to the jailer. From these men we shall expect answers, to be published in our next issue.

We do not take this stand on this one case so much on account of itself, but on account of the principle involved. It has been altogether too customary for county officers to learn "what there was in it," receive their divvy and keep mum. Especially is this the case when one county is joined to another for judicial purposes as Billings is to Morton. All the officers of the older counties cared for was to run up as much costs as possible on the unorganized counties, get their share of the plunder and then like a squeezed lemon, throw the rind away.

We have had enough of this outside interference in our affairs and want to give notice that Billings county's affairs shall not be tampered with by any blood-suckers, legalized or not. A perfectly honest administration of our affairs by Morton county must and shall be had. Any other outside interference is liable to leave the meddler with badly burned fingers.

When we have received an answer as to how and by whose authority this criminal was released, we will have a few other questions to ask relative to other matters.
articles.summary: Packard demands an explanation of how a man arrested by Wm. Jones for setting a prairie fire near Scoria came to be released from the Mandan jail, and warns Morton county officers against plundering Billings county.

articles.headline: Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text:
STOCK NOTES.

From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the COW BOY office.
articles.summary: Stray notice: John Pohl's bay horse, branded with an anchor, a hat and a Texas 7N brand, strayed from Little Missouri July 6, 1884; $25 reward.

articles.text:
Below are the three round-up districts in which our cowmen are interested. They will be kept standing until they begin. It will be noticed that the Powder river round-up begins May 7 and the Yellowstone and Little Missouri begin May 25:

ROUND-UP DISTRCT No. 5.

Beginning at the mouth of Powder river, May 7, 1885; thence working down the Yellowstone river on the south side to the mouth of O'Fallon creek; thence up O'Fallon creek and its tributaries to its head; thence across to the head of Little Beaver; thence down Little Beaver to within ten miles of its mouth: thence across to the head of Big Beaver; thence down Big Beaver to the Northern Pacific railroad; thence across to the head of Glendive creek and down to the Yellowstone river; thence up the Yellowstone river including Cedar creek to the mouth of Cabin creek; thence up Cabin creek to its head. J. H. Lander, foreman.

ROUND-UP DISTRICT No. 6.

Beginning at the mouth of Box Elder, May 25, 1885; thence working down the Little Missouri and its tributaries to a point about twenty miles below the mouth of Big Beaver; thence up Big Beaver and its tributaries to the Northern Pacific railroad. W. P. Osterhout, foreman.

ROUND-UP DISTRICT No. 7.

Beginning May 25, 1885, at the mouth of the Yellowstone river, thence working up the Yellowstone river and tributaries on the east side to Glendive and the Northern Pacific railroad. R. H. Moore, foreman.
articles.summary: Standing notice of round-up districts 5, 6 and 7: Powder river round-up begins May 7, Little Missouri and Yellowstone round-ups May 25.

articles.text: From every direction comes news of the pressing necessity for draft horses, especially those averaging over twelve hundred. The raising of these horses is an industry that has even less chance of being overdone than that of raising cattle.
articles.summary: Note on the demand for heavy draft horses.

articles.text: The Shorthorns, formerly often called Durhams, came from northeastern England, and are the most numerous and mostly widely distributed breed in this country, or in the world. The size is of the largest; the color is either red, white, or a mixture of either of these in any proportion. The horn is short and comparatively light, but no more so than in some other breeds. Although valued chiefly as a beef-making animal, Shorthorns as a breed are good milkers, but less attention has been given of late years to their dairy qualities than formerly. No cattle are more attractive than the best Shorthorns. The body is long, the back straight and broad, the ribs well sprung, the rump straight and well filled out. As a rule Shorthorns are taller than cattle of most other breeds, and not infrequently they are subject to the criticisms of being too long in the leg. The head and neck are generally light and well formed. The beef is good and the milk is of full average richness. No other breed has had anything like the influence on the cattle in the chief beef-producing States as the Shorthorn.—[N. W. Farmer.
articles.summary: Reprinted description of the Shorthorn breed, from the N. W. Farmer.

articles.text: At the risk of hammering too often on one nail, we will say a word more on the subject of cheap bulls. We think that breeders generally will concur in the opinion that, as a rule, cheap bulls, in the sense in which we now use the term cheap, "dear at any price," would perhaps be the most correct expression of our meaning, have wrought more harm to the cause of pure breeding than aught else in the history of livestock development. It is to utter a mere truism to say that the bull is the most important part of the herd; that while an inferior cow stamps her impress upon but one calf in a season, the inferior bull will deteriorate the whole season's crop of calves. These things are so plain that to emphasize them is to be tedious, and yet of all things worth remembering none seem so easily forgotten. We have seen inferior bulls sold at less money than could have been obtained for them as steers at the same age, and they brought too high a price then. It is the great mistake which so many make, to imagine that the registry makes the bull. Registry is the certificate upon which we base our faith in the animal's pure breeding, and as far as that goes it is not only desirable but essential, but when it comes to merit we must look to the animal itself, and to its record as a calf-getter. The difference in the quality of a bull will readily make a difference of $200 to $400, or $500 in the value of the first crop of calves, and the greatest mistake a man can make is to deceive himself on the importance of getting a good bull, and equally great, and still more culpable is the mistake of the breeder who permits himself to sell inferior bulls that he knows are not fit to breed from. It is a suicidal policy, and unfortunately one that affects all breeders as well as himself.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted article against cheap and inferior bulls, from the National Live Stock Journal.

articles.text: "Experience is a dear teacher," but from some remarks we have heard, the losses on late states' yearlings has not had its full weight on some of our stockmen. From points gathered from all sources we will state it as a fact that outside of late one's and two's the loss in the Bad Lands has not been two per cent. This includes all cattle brought in early last spring and old cattle. At least three per cent., if not more, of the late one's and two's succumbed to their ignorance of the ranges and of how to rustle. In view of these facts it certainly seems foolish to hear stockmen say that there is plenty of time to put in cattle later in the season and that they will contract for some after a while. "Now is the accepted time" to contract and inside of a month every head of cattle should be on the range, that is expected to winter here in safety.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy reports winter losses in the Bad Lands under two per cent except among late-shipped yearlings and two-year-olds, and urges stockmen to contract for cattle now.

articles.text: The arrival of a shipment of cattle at the Union Stock Yards, Chicago, last Friday, from Walla Walla, Washington Territory, marked something like an epoch in western cattle trade, this being the first shipment of cattle ever made to the Chicago market from the Pacific coast. The drove in question numbered 330, and averaged 1,294 lbs.; they brought $4.40 per 100 lbs., a price which was declared satisfactory to their owners. The cattle were range cattle, and had left Walla Walla by train March 30th, and arrived in Chicago April 10th, having been eleven days on the way. They, of course, made the whole distance, nearly 2,300 miles, by rail, and were unloaded but five times; they traveled over four great railways, and through three of the largest territories and three of the largest states. While there was no great profit, taken altogether, as an experimental shipment, it was a success. Only one animal was lost, its horns being caught between the slats of the car, and in trying to free itself it was strangled. The cattle were bought for the dressed beef trade, and if they should be destined to make up some of the orders for the supply of British troops, it is more than likely that they may reach, before fulfilling their ultimate destiny, the mountains of Afghanistan, after traveling more than half way around the world.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted report of the first shipment of range cattle from Walla Walla to the Chicago stock yards.

articles.text: When the Polled-Angus and Hereford association met in Chicago, last fall, the call was made on the members at both meetings to agree to steer some pure-bred bull calves for the purpose of preparing them for future exhibits. The call resulted in members of the last named, although it was a very full meeting, agreeing to steer thirteen bull calves, and the members of the Angus association agreeing to steer sixteen. Members present expressed themselves as encouraged by this readiness (?) of members to sacrifice males for the benefit of the breed. One would certainly be justified from this in supposing that the great majority of those present regarded every male calf dropped as fit to breed from. Yet there is not one of the gentlemen present who does not cordially concur in the advice so frequently given to breeders, to "use the knife unsparingly." It is, then, as in so many other things, simply a question of temporary profit. It is true pure-bred bulls are better than scrubs any day in the year, and that the number of pure-bred bulls is comparatively insignificant in proportion to the whole number of cattle in the country. It is also doubtless true that our pure-bred cattle probably average higher than they do in other countries, owing to the fact that so many of them have been imported, and it is presumable that importers, if they have not always secured the best, have rarely, if ever, undertaken to bring over inferior animals. At the same time, it is useless to deny that breeders are setting but a poor example to the numerous farmers who are using, or offering for service, grade bulls, when they decline to use the knife on any of their pure-bred animals, and every year send out some which they well know themselves will do little or no credit to the breed itself or to themselves, as breeders. As nothing does the breeder so much good as the get of the bulls he sells in the neighborhoods where they go, if they are a credit to him and his bulls, so nothing permanently injures his reputation more surely than to send out an inferior bull, sold exclusively on the strength of his being registered. We hope, during the next few months, to hear of many pure-bred bull calves put in the way of being converted into prime beef.—[National L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted article urging breeders to steer inferior pure-bred bull calves, from the National Live Stock Journal.

articles.headline: Sporting Notes.
articles.text:
Kittleman is again raking in the shekals in California on his hundred yard time.

Dan Mace, probably the best trainer and driver of trotting horses this country has ever produced, died April 19. Among other horses he brought out and gave records to Lady Thorne, American Girl, G. M. Patchen, Pocahontas, Ethan Allen, Judge Fullerton, Medoc, George Wilkes and Fearnaught.

Sullivan has kept up his hippodroming and deceitfulness so long that all his backers are losing confidence in him. He and Ryan have signed articles to fight at Butte City, Montana, but it is money to marbles that the fight never takes place. Sullivan will have few sympathizers should he lose the championship.
articles.summary: Sporting notes: Kittleman sprinting in California, death of trotting-horse trainer Dan Mace on April 19, and doubts about a Sullivan–Ryan fight at Butte City.

articles.text: E. Elmer is building a dwelling house on Williamson & Copeland's lot.
articles.summary: E. Elmer is building a dwelling on Williamson & Copeland's lot.

articles.text: To-day is the last chance for contestants in the shooting match in the rink.
articles.summary: Last day of the shooting match at the rink.

articles.text: The historical shack just vacated by Dr. Jorgens is already rented for a dry-goods and clothing store.
articles.summary: The shack vacated by Dr. Jorgens is rented for a dry-goods and clothing store.

articles.text: L. Ayers again loomed up on us yesterday. He is always welcome to Medora, where he has a host of friends.
articles.summary: L. Ayers visited Medora.

articles.text: It is estimated that 150,000 cattle will be shipped into Montana and the Bad Lands of Dakota this summer.
articles.summary: Estimate that 150,000 cattle will be shipped into Montana and the Bad Lands this summer.

articles.text: About one hundred men will be employed constantly at the slaughter-house as soon as the season's work begins.
articles.summary: About a hundred men will work at the slaughter-house.

articles.text: Peter Book is building a fine dwelling house near his brick kiln. He will veneer it as soon as he can make the brick.
articles.summary: Peter Book is building a dwelling near his brick kiln.

articles.text: F. D. Foster started for Chicago this morning after his wife, and a lot of men to work in the slaughter-house. He will return in about three weeks.
articles.summary: F. D. Foster left for Chicago to bring back his wife and slaughter-house workers.

articles.text: What we want to know is whether Johnny Munro has been and gone and done it or not. Any information will be cheerfully received at this office.
articles.summary: Joking inquiry whether Johnny Munro has "been and gone and done it."

articles.text: Remember that the masquerade at the rink will take place Saturday night. Those who attended the last one will need no invitation to come again.
articles.summary: A masquerade will be held at the rink Saturday night.

articles.text: Mr. Paddock finds that his livery barn is altogether too small for his business, although it is of good size, and intends immediately to about double its size.
articles.summary: Mr. Paddock plans to double the size of his livery barn.

articles.text: Mr. Jordan's wife and daughter arrived from the east last week and the family will go to keeping house as soon as a dwelling, already begun, is completed.
articles.summary: Mr. Jordan's wife and daughter arrived from the east.

articles.text: T. L. Skinner, attorney for the Caledonia mine in the Hills, went out on this morning's coach. He has been in New Orleans in charge of the Black Hills exhibit.
articles.summary: T. L. Skinner, attorney for the Caledonia mine, left for the Black Hills by coach.

articles.text: A large number of cattle have been contracted for by the Marquis, the principal firms contracted with being the Hashknife and Niobrara companies. About 20,000 will be delivered here this summer and fall.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès has contracted with the Hashknife and Niobrara companies for about 20,000 cattle to be delivered at Medora.

articles.text: "Oh, its nice to be a daddy," sings Frank Keeler. In confidence, he admits that it is the prettiest little ten-pound male cherub in the country and was born April 11. Mrs. Keeler will come to Medora to live in about two weeks.
articles.summary: Frank Keeler's son was born April 11; Mrs. Keeler will move to Medora.

articles.text: The stock-yards across the river are of very little use, being entirely too small. They should be four times as large and have a good branding chute. Should the railroad company not improve the yards, it would pay our stockmen to do so.
articles.summary: The stock-yards across the river are too small and need a branding chute.

articles.text: Foot-ball and base-ball are becoming popular sports among the boys. If a nine were organized anywhere between Dickinson and Glendive, or even at a further distance where expenses were guaranteed, we could make it very warm for them.
articles.summary: Foot-ball and base-ball are popular with Medora boys.

articles.text: Our readers will notice the new advertisment of the Fargo Ins. Co., appearing in this issue. This is a perfectly safe and reliable company having a paid-up capital of $100,000. It should be patronized extensively as it is a home institution.
articles.summary: Notice of the new Fargo Insurance Co. advertisement.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens and Mr. Martin have been busy moving the drug-store for a day or two and are now nearly settled in the best store room in town. It is of good size, painted in light colors and has a full glass front. We hope to see other stores as good go up speedily.
articles.summary: The drug store has moved into a new store room with a full glass front.

articles.text: And it came to pass that William the bronco-buster bet Johnny he could ride a bucking cayuse. But William was afflicted sore and he did pound a hole in the ground which in the wet season will fill up and become like unto a lake. And a glittering shekal did pass from the hand of William to that of Johnny and after a season of barter gurgled down the throats of those who had come forth to see. And all grinned gleefully.
articles.summary: Mock-scriptural account of William the bronco-buster losing a bet to Johnny after being thrown by a bucking cayuse.

articles.text: Wm. Jones, an old-time college mate of the editor's, is now private secretary to the Marquis. There is no one of our friends whom we wish or who deserves greater success.
articles.summary: Wm. Jones, the editor's old college mate, is now private secretary to the Marquis de Morès.

articles.text: It is now the intention of the Co. to put up a large lodging house, capable of accommodating all the slaughter-house men. It will be put up as soon as the brick can be made.
articles.summary: The Company plans a large brick lodging house for slaughter-house men.

articles.text: Two duck hunters from Medora were badly disappointed in getting ducks at Beach last Saturday, but their disappointment was greatly lessened by the pleasure of a very enjoyable dance held at the section house under the auspices of Mrs. Gustin and Miss.
articles.summary: Medora duck hunters attended a dance at the Beach section house.

articles.text: The Willard Bros. arrived Monday evening with one of the best herds of horses that has ever been driven in here. They were a long time in the cars and many had their manes and tails eaten off, but as a whole they showed up well. Several head were sold here but they were too late to strike the market. They [start?] to-day or to-marrow for the Hills and will reach there in about sixteen days.
articles.summary: The Willard Bros. arrived with a herd of horses bound for the Black Hills.

articles.text: T. K. Long prosecuting attorney of Morton county and Ed. Drury, deputy sheriff came up Sunday night to enforce the law passed during the last legislature, compelling the liquor dealers of unorganized counties to pay a county license to the senior counties. Partial payments were made by the liquor men and the whole will probably be paid. We very much doubt the constitutionality of this law and by all means advise our liquor men to make a test case and fight it out. It is worth the trial in any event and this is undoubtly only an entering wedge to further taxation.
articles.summary: Morton county officers came to collect county liquor licenses from Medora dealers; the Cow Boy urges a test case.

articles.text: A meeting to organize a bucket brigade was held in the rink last Monday evening. It was called to order by J. C. Fisher and A. T. Packard was elected chairman. The necessity of such an organization was unanimously conceded. On motion, a committee of five was appointed, the names of J. C. Fisher, Jos. A. Ferris, Marquis de Mores, F. D. Foster and J. B. Walker being suggested and adopted. This committee was authorized to go ahead and perfect all arrangements. They met Tuesday evening and decided to purchase buckets, ladders, hooks, axes &c., the money to be raised by subscription. The force-pump and pipe at the Marquis' house may also be brought into requisition.
articles.summary: A bucket brigade was organized at the rink with A. T. Packard as chairman and a committee including the Marquis de Morès.
